t: Groups of Special-Equivalent Strings — Canonical Signature via Even/Odd Character Counts
o:
## Understanding the problem

We may freely permute characters at even indices among themselves, and independently permute characters at odd indices. So two strings are special-equivalent exactly when they contain the same multiset of characters at even positions **and** the same multiset at odd positions. We must count the number of equivalence classes (groups) in `words`.

**Example 1:** `"abcd"`, `"cdab"`, `"cbad"` all have even-index multiset `{a,c}` and odd-index multiset `{b,d}`, so they form one group. `"xyzz"` and `"zzxy"` share even `{x,z}` and odd `{y,z}` — a second group. `"zzyx"` has even `{z,x}` but odd `{z,y}` — a third group. Answer: 3.

**Example 2:** every permutation of `abc` keeps even multiset `{a,c}` and odd multiset `{b}` for strings of length 3 starting/ending appropriately... checking each: `abc`,`acb`,`bac`,`bca`,`cab`,`cba` split into 3 distinct (even,odd) signature pairs, so the answer is 3.

Constraints are tiny ($n \le 1000$, length $\le 20$), so even an $O(n^2)$ pairwise comparison works; the clean solution is to map each string to a canonical key and count distinct keys.
k: Swaps only happen within even indices or within odd indices, so the two parity classes never mix.
Two strings are special-equivalent iff their sorted even-position characters equal AND their sorted odd-position characters equal.
Counting groups = counting distinct canonical signatures, solvable with a hash set.

a.i: For each pair of strings, test special-equivalence directly by sorting the even-indexed substring and the odd-indexed substring of both and comparing. Mark visited strings and count connected components of this equivalence relation. With $n \le 1000$ this is fast enough, though it does redundant work compared to hashing signatures.
s: Define equivalent(a, b): sorted even chars of a == sorted even chars of b and same for odd chars.
Iterate i over words; if words[i] already grouped, skip.
Otherwise increment group count and scan all j > i, grouping any word[j] equivalent to words[i].
a.t: O(n * L log L) per string for building signatures; a true pairwise brute force would be O(n^2 * L log L), still fine for n <= 1000.
a.sp: O(n * L) for the hash set of signatures.

a.i: Instead of sorting substrings, build a fixed-size key from character counts: 26 counters for even positions and 26 for odd positions. Two strings are special-equivalent iff these two count vectors match, since swaps can realize any permutation within each parity class. This gives an O(L) signature per string with no sorting.
s: For each word, create two arrays of size 26, one for even indices, one for odd indices.
Increment the appropriate counter for each character based on index parity.
Flatten both counters into a single tuple/string key and insert into a hash set.
Return the size of the set.
a.t: O(n * L) total — each character is processed once to build its signature; hashing the fixed-size key is O(1).
a.sp: O(n * 52) for storing up to n distinct constant-size signatures.

w:
## Wrap-up

In an interview, lead with the observation that parity classes never mix, then present the canonical-signature approach — either sorted even/odd substrings or 52-slot counters — and count distinct keys with a set. The counter version is optimal at $O(n \cdot L)$ time.

**Pitfalls:** forgetting that position parity is defined by original index (not after any transformation); using a single combined multiset instead of separate even/odd multisets (this wrongly merges groups like `"zzxy"` vs `"zzyx"`); when encoding counts as characters, ensure counts fit in one byte (length ≤ 20 guarantees this).

**Edge cases:** single-character words (all identical words form one group); all words mutually equivalent → answer 1; all distinct signatures → answer n.

**Follow-ups:** what if swaps could also exchange an even and an odd character (then just compare full multisets)? What if words had different lengths (parity alignment breaks — need case-by-case reasoning)?
